clue.text: T Blair seen wandering around old part of capital

indicators.note: letters that go wandering around leave their places, so the three words before it are rearranged

parts.note: taken as written: these ten letters are the ones rearranged

explanation.surface: Tony Blair is spotted strolling through a historic quarter of a capital city.
explanation.walkthrough: 'wandering around' is the anagram signal for T BLAIR SEEN. 'Old' is fair because the German capital was reunited in 1990, so its eastern half is no longer a separate part.
explanation.definitionFit: From 1949 to 1990 the Soviet-sector half of Germany's divided chief city was a separate entity, the seat of the German Democratic Republic.

clue.text: Different golfer on start of eighteenth

indicators.note: in a down entry the piece that is on another is written above it, so the golfer's name comes first

parts.note: Ernie Els is a South African golfer who has won four major championships

indicators.note: the start of a word is its opening letter, so only the first letter of eighteenth is used

explanation.surface: An unusual golfer stands at the beginning of the eighteenth hole.
explanation.walkthrough: ELS is Ernie Els, the South African golfer setters love. 'on' in a down clue stacks him above the E that 'start of' takes from eighteenth.
explanation.definitionFit: Synonym when it follows a pronoun or question word: it marks a thing as other than the one already mentioned.

clue.text: Flaky guy losing form in heat

definitions.text: Flaky guy losing form in heat

parts.words: Flaky guy losing form in heat
parts.note: read literally: a man-shaped figure made of frozen flakes, which melts out of shape when the weather turns warm

explanation.surface: An unreliable sportsman goes off his game during a qualifying race.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface is an erratic athlete off his game in a qualifying race. Literally, 'flaky' is made of flakes, 'losing form' is melting out of shape and 'heat' is warm weather.
explanation.definitionFit: A cryptic description: the winter figure children build is made of frozen flakes and melts out of shape once the temperature rises.

clue.text: The ins and outs of domestic finance

definitions.text: The ins and outs of domestic finance

parts.words: The ins and outs of domestic finance
parts.note: read literally: a record of the money coming into and going out of a household's account, not the fine detail of a subject

explanation.surface: All the fine detail of how a household manages its money.
explanation.walkthrough: 'The ins and outs' normally means the intricate details of a subject. Here it is literal: the payments in and the payments out, listed on the regular record of a personal account.
explanation.definitionFit: A cryptic description: the document lists every deposit into and withdrawal from a personal account, the literal incomings and outgoings of household money.

clue.text: Backing a typical financial district to display greed

indicators.note: backing a vehicle means sending it backwards, so the two pieces after it are written back to front as one run

parts.note: taken as written
par is the usual or expected standard, as in 'par for the course'
the City is the name of London's financial district, the Square Mile

explanation.surface: Supporting an ordinary banking quarter as a way of showing avarice.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Backing' reads as supporting, but it turns A PAR round to make RAPA. The City, with a capital C, is London's financial quarter; 'to display' only links the wordplay to the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Synonym: both nouns name grasping avarice, an excessive appetite for money or possessions.

clue.text: Model fish on a line

indicators.note: in a down entry the piece that is on the others is written above them, so the fish comes first

parts.note: the ide is a freshwater fish of the carp family, a crossword regular
taken as written
L is the abbreviation for line, used in references to lines of text

explanation.surface: A toy fish dangling from an angler's line.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface is a toy fish on an angler's line, but 'Model' is the adjective meaning perfect. 'on' in a down clue puts IDE above A and L.
explanation.definitionFit: Synonym as an adjective: a model pupil is a perfect one, exactly what one would wish for.

clue.text: School on river making racket

indicators.note: on here simply attaches one piece to the other: the school's letter is set against the river's name

parts.note: S is a dictionary abbreviation for school (it is listed in Collins)
the Cam is the river that flows through Cambridge in eastern England

explanation.surface: A school beside a river is producing a dreadful din.
explanation.walkthrough: 'racket' in the surface is the din of noisy pupils; the definition is its other sense, a swindle. 'on' joins S to CAM, the river that runs through Cambridge.
explanation.definitionFit: Synonym in the criminal sense: a dishonest scheme for making money, a swindle or fraud.

clue.text: Diagram includes one old vehicle

indicators.note: the diagram word includes the next two pieces, so they are placed inside its letters

parts.note: a chart is a diagram that sets information out visually
I is the Roman numeral for one
O is the standard abbreviation for old, as in OT for Old Testament

explanation.surface: A technical drawing that features a single vintage car.
explanation.walkthrough: 'old vehicle' looks like the definition, but 'old' is needed for the O, leaving just 'vehicle'. 'includes' puts I and O inside CHART.
explanation.definitionFit: Example: the two-wheeled horse-drawn carriage of ancient warfare and racing is one kind of conveyance.

clue.text: Person in court showing mother point made to judge

parts.note: ma is an informal word for mother
the gist of an argument is its essential point
to rate something is to judge its worth

explanation.surface: Someone at a hearing lets their mother see the argument put to the judge.
explanation.walkthrough: The whole surface stays in the courtroom, which hides that 'point' and 'judge' are separate pieces: GIST, the main point, and RATE, to judge or assess. 'showing' and 'made to' only join things up.
explanation.definitionFit: Example: a justice of the peace, who hears minor cases in the lower courts of England and Wales, is one such figure on the bench.

clue.text: Cut from small musical instrument

parts.note: S is the abbreviation for small, as on clothing labels
a horn is a brass instrument that is blown

explanation.surface: Something sliced off a miniature instrument.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Cut' reads as a noun or a command in the surface; as the definition it is the past participle, describing hair or wool that has been clipped off. 'from' leads to the wordplay.
explanation.definitionFit: Synonym as a past participle: hair or wool that has been sheared has been clipped off close.

clue.text: One could have made you serve old workers in fleet street

definitions.text: One could have made you serve
definitions.meaning: a naval detachment that once seized men in ports and forced them to serve as sailors
Fleet Street in London was long the home of Britain's national newspapers, so its former staff were the newspaper crowd

explanation.surface: Someone might once have forced you to wait on retired newspaper staff.
explanation.walkthrough: Two definitions: the naval band that forced men into service, and whimsically the journalists who once worked in London's Fleet Street, former home of Britain's newspapers. Lower-case 'fleet' also winks at the navy.
explanation.definitionFit: Historically a naval detachment that forced men into service; whimsically, the crowd of journalists who once worked in London's newspaper district.

clue.text: Send a rude chef away enjoying his misery?

indicators.note: letters sent away leave their places, so the four words before it are rearranged

parts.note: taken as written: thirteen letters to rearrange

explanation.surface: Dismissing an ill-mannered cook and taking pleasure in his distress.
explanation.walkthrough: 'away' is the anagram signal for SEND A RUDE CHEF. The question mark excuses a definition by example: 'his' is the chef of the surface, standing for anyone whose bad luck is relished.
explanation.definitionFit: The German loanword names the pleasure taken in somebody else's misfortune, here the sacked cook's.

clue.text: Standing up for the losers of this tuneful party game

definitions.text: Standing up for the losers of this tuneful party game

parts.words: Standing up for the losers of this tuneful party game
parts.note: read literally: in this children's game played to music, whoever is left on their feet without a seat when the tune stops is out

explanation.surface: Defending the underdogs in a party game with music.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Standing up for the losers' sounds like defending the underdogs. Literally, the players who lose are the ones left on their feet when the music stops and there is one seat too few.
explanation.definitionFit: A cryptic description: children circle while a tune plays and scramble to sit when it stops; whoever is left on their feet is out.

clue.text: Sailors shouldn't be working on this

definitions.text: Sailors shouldn't be working on this

parts.words: Sailors shouldn't be working on this
parts.note: read literally: the time off a ship's crew is allowed to spend on land, during which nobody is on duty

explanation.surface: A job or piece of equipment that seamen ought to keep their hands off.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface suggests a task or a piece of kit that sailors ought to leave alone. 'This' is really a spell of time: a crew's permitted break on dry land, when nobody is on duty.
explanation.definitionFit: A cryptic description: it is the permitted time a ship's crew spends on land, off duty and free of their tasks.

clue.text: Groom Henry and pat? They won't be there!

indicators.note: to groom is to tidy and put in order, so the letters of the two names after it are put into a new order

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: The bridegroom, Henry and Pat will all be missing from the event.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Groom' looks like the bridegroom but is a verb, the anagram signal for HENRY and PAT. The definition leans on the surface: 'They' are the groom and his male friends, barred from a bride's all-female celebration.
explanation.definitionFit: A cryptic description: in Britain this is the bride's all-female celebration before her wedding, so the groom and other men are absent.

clue.text: Bumpy ride to be one in charge of 10?

indicators.note: a bumpy journey shakes things about, so the letters of the two words after it are jolted into a new order

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A rough passage lies ahead for whoever is to run Number 10.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bumpy' is the anagram signal for RIDE TO. '10' is not Downing Street but a cross-reference: the answer at 10 across can be read as a newspaper's staff, and this is their boss.
explanation.definitionFit: The answer at 10 across reads as a band of newspaper journalists, and this person heads a paper and directs them.

clue.text: Unconvincing presentation that may have strings attached

definitions.meaning: a figurative dictionary sense: a stagy, specious show that fools nobody
the literal art: shows given with marionettes, figures worked from above by strings

explanation.surface: A feeble sales pitch that may come with awkward conditions.
explanation.walkthrough: Two senses of one word: Collins gives 'unconvincing or specious presentation' as a figurative meaning, and the second half is literal, since marionettes are worked by strings. In the surface 'strings attached' means awkward conditions.
explanation.definitionFit: Figuratively a stagy, specious display; literally the art of working marionettes, which dangle from cords held by the operator.

clue.text: Black sheep's first one making thrust

indicators.note: first says the sheep's word leads, going in front of the word for black although the clue names black earlier

parts.note: a ram is a male sheep
jet is a deep glossy black, as in jet-black hair

explanation.surface: The family outcast is the first to make a lunge.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Black sheep' is not the family outcast: the two words are clued separately, and 'first' means the sheep's word leads even though black is named earlier. 'Thrust' is an engine's propulsive force, not a lunge.
explanation.definitionFit: It is a simple type of aircraft engine that uses its own forward speed to compress incoming air and so generate propulsive force.

clue.text: Command chap to be accompanied by boyfriend

indicators.note: a piece that is accompanied by another has it alongside, so the boyfriend word follows the chap word

parts.note: chap is informal British English for a man
someone's date is the person they are going out with, such as a boyfriend

explanation.surface: Order a fellow to bring his boyfriend along.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface is an order to a fellow about his partner. 'to be accompanied by' sets DATE beside MAN; 'Command' is the definition, as a noun (an official instruction) or as a verb (to require).
explanation.definitionFit: Synonym as noun or verb: an authoritative order, or to require something officially.

clue.text: You have rotisserie but how to get gratuities?

indicators.note: the question asks for a method, so what is wanted is an instruction that would produce the word that follows

parts.note: gratuities are TIPS, and that word appears when SPIT, a roasting rod, is written backwards

explanation.surface: You own a rotisserie, but what will bring in the tips?
explanation.walkthrough: A reverse clue: 'how to get' asks for an instruction. Gratuities are TIPS, and you get TIPS by turning SPIT round; the definition is 'rotisserie', a roasting rod that rotates.
explanation.definitionFit: Both name a roasting device whose rod rotates meat before the heat; the older word also meant the servant or dog that worked it.

clue.text: Use rod with whip on beast

indicators.note: with sets the whip word alongside the rod word, following it

parts.note: to pole a punt is to push it along with a long rod
the cat is the cat-o'-nine-tails, a whip with nine knotted cords once used for flogging in the navy

explanation.surface: Beating an animal with a stick and a lash.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface is cruelty to an animal. 'Use rod' is the verb POLE, to push a punt along, and 'with' adds CAT, short for the cat-o'-nine-tails, a naval flogging whip.
explanation.definitionFit: Example: a dark-furred wild relative of the ferret, notorious for its foul smell, is one kind of animal.

clue.text: He might get short colonel car park if ordered

indicators.note: letters that are ordered are put into a particular sequence, so what precedes is rearranged
a phrase that is short stops early, losing its final letter

parts.note: taken as written, before the cut
the final letter of park, the one that is lost

explanation.surface: He could find a parking space for a diminutive colonel if told to.
explanation.walkthrough: 'short' takes the final K from COLONEL CAR PARK and 'if ordered' rearranges the thirteen letters left. The definition is just 'He': a junior soldier in the British Army, who would do a colonel's bidding.
explanation.definitionFit: The pronoun points at a soldier of the lowest non-commissioned rank in the British Army, who takes orders from officers such as a colonel.

clue.text: Old black priest showing signs of doubt

parts.note: O is the standard abbreviation for old, as in OE for Old English
B is the abbreviation for black, as on soft pencils and in chess
Eli is the Old Testament high priest who raised Samuel, the setters' favourite priest

explanation.surface: An elderly priest in black letting his wavering faith show.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface is an elderly cleric whose faith is visibly wavering. The definition is literal: these are the dagger-like marks that editors print beside passages they suspect are not genuine.
explanation.definitionFit: Plural of the dagger-shaped mark that scribes and editors set beside a passage they suspect is spurious.

clue.text: Cost includes tenor for gala

indicators.note: the cost word includes the tenor's letter, which therefore goes inside it

parts.note: a fee is the cost charged for a service
T is the abbreviation for tenor in choral music, as in SATB

explanation.surface: The price covers hiring a tenor to sing at the gala.
explanation.walkthrough: 'includes' puts T inside FEE. In Britain the answer is above all a village fair with stalls and games, though it also covers any festive occasion; 'for' links to the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Synonym: both are festive public occasions, celebrations with entertainments often held outdoors.

clue.text: Separated chaps with time to see pad

indicators.note: with adds the next piece alongside, after the word for chaps

parts.note: a couple who are separated are living apart
chaps is informal British English for men
T is the standard abbreviation for time, as in physics formulae

explanation.surface: Men who have split from their partners find a spare moment to view a flat.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Pad' is slang for the place where someone lives. 'with' adds T after MEN, and 'to see' only leads from the wordplay to the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Slang synonym: someone's pad is their flat, a set of rooms to live in.

clue.text: Relative's corrupt, abandoning one

indicators.note: the corrupt word is abandoning, that is giving up, the letters that stand for one

parts.note: unclean means morally impure, so corrupt
an is the indefinite article, another way of saying one

explanation.surface: A family member is crooked and is deserting somebody.
explanation.walkthrough: 'abandoning' takes AN, one, off the end of UNCLEAN. The apostrophe-s is short for 'is', joining the definition to the wordplay.
explanation.definitionFit: Example: a parent's brother, or an aunt's husband, is one kind of family member.

clue.text: Beer maker dropping brother's jug

indicators.note: the beer maker is dropping, that is losing, the letters that stand for brother

parts.note: a brewer is someone who makes beer
Br is the abbreviation for Brother, the title of a monk or friar

explanation.surface: A brewer lets his brother's pitcher slip from his hands.
explanation.walkthrough: In the surface the jug is the brother's and gets dropped. Really 'dropping' takes BR off the front of BREWER, and what is left is the jug.
explanation.definitionFit: Synonym: a large wide-mouthed pitcher for carrying water, once kept in bedrooms for washing.

clue.text: Downtown and a way to describe it!

indicators.note: the phrase promises a description of the word that follows, one that locates its letters inside another word

parts.note: the letters I and T are the middle pair of the four-letter word for a large town, so naming the heart of that word describes them

explanation.surface: The downtown area, plus one means of characterising it.
explanation.walkthrough: A reverse clue: 'a way to describe' asks for a phrase that would clue the last word. IT is the centre of CITY, so the answer literally describes 'it'; 'Downtown' is the American word for the place.
explanation.definitionFit: Synonym across dialects: the American term for a town's central business and shopping district, which British speakers name this way.
